newsitem.title: USA: U.S sour crude under pressure from imports, SPR.
newsitem.headline: U.S sour crude under pressure from imports, SPR.

text.p: U.S. heavy sour crudes are under assault from an influx of regional Canadian imports, a series of refinery hiccups and the U.S. government's sale of oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) this week, oil trades said.
"Midwest sours are getting pressured by alternatives from Canada and California, plus refiners backing out barrels," a crude trader in the Midwest said.
Others confirmed they sold large quantities of West Texas Sour/Midland after news that Petroleos de Venezuela shut down a 108,000 bpd catcracker at its Amuay refinery this week.
Pressure already mounted last week when BP America's 136,000 bpd Toledo, Ohio refinery reduced crude runs after a fire brought down a crude and vacuum distillation unit.
Traders also speculated that Koch Oil's 236,000 bpd Pine Bend, Minnesota refinery might be undergoing maintenance as they sold down West Texas Sour. Koch won't comment.
The grade dropped to a discount of $1.68 a barrel against West Texas Intermediate/Cushing on Wednesday, compared with a $1.32 a barrel discount last week.
Californian crudes piped into the Midwest were also blamed for displacing West Texas Sour more than Gulf Coast Eugene Island, which eased by a lesser amount.
Canadian crude imports last week rose 771,000 barrels for PADD's 1 through 4, to 1.1 million barrels, according to the American Petroleum Institute (API) report.
Pipeline operators confirmed the higher flows, dismissing talk refiners might be slowing purchases amid high prices.
"Throughputs to the U.S. have not been reduced, flows have not been cut back," said Alan Roth, spokesman for Canada's IPL Pipeline, adding that pumping was at projected capacity.
Refiners were still keeping operating capacities high in order to maximize heating oil production, and lower gasoline stocks also renewed incentive to push the incremental barrel.
Average Gulf Coast pre-tax profit margins for the third quarter this year were $1.03 a barrel, down from the prior year's $1.47, according to consultancy Bonner & Moore.
Anemic margins, however, appear set to improve over the fourth quarter, estimated around $1.33 a barrel.
"The rise will come from heating oil and gasoline holding up a little better, and also residual fuel," said Charles McSpadden, Bonner & Moore's vice-president of market analysis.
The current drive to produce light products now has only abetted the divergence in sweet and sour grades.
That differential between Light Louisiana Sweet and West Texas Sour is at its widest in two years, traders said.
